title: Archaeologist looks into sealed chamber of golden treasures
dek: Howard Carter peers by candlelight into a crowded chamber of Tutankhamun’s tomb in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings.
body:
In the Valley of the Kings this afternoon, British archaeologist Howard Carter cleared the last rubble from a descending passage and reached a second sealed doorway. He made a small breach near the top left corner, tested the air with a candle, and looked inside. Lord Carnarvon, Lady Evelyn Herbert and the engineer Arthur Callender waited beside him.

Hot air from the chamber made the flame flicker. As his eyes adjusted, a crowded room of extraordinary objects appeared: two ebony statues of a king in gold sandals, gilded animal-shaped couches, painted caskets, a golden throne and many other furnishings heaped together. Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything. Carter answered that it was wonderful. He then widened the hole and, with an electric torch as well as another candle, let the others look in. A further sealed door stood between the two statues.

The plaster seals carried the name of Tutankhamun, a little-known pharaoh of the eighteenth dynasty who had ruled only briefly more than three thousand years earlier. The outer stairway had been found on 4 November. Carter refilled it for safety and cabled Carnarvon in England. The earl arrived in Luxor a few days ago. Marks of ancient damage and repair on the doors had suggested robbers might have emptied the place, yet the objects still packed inside showed that any earlier entry had been stopped short.

Carter, who came to Egypt as a young artist and later worked as an inspector of antiquities, had searched this ground for years with Carnarvon’s money. Many experts believed the valley held nothing more. One last season, begun at the start of November, uncovered the steps just as that support was about to end. Listing, photographing and conserving every object, and opening whatever lies beyond, will now require long and careful seasons of work.

The discovery still matters because almost no other New Kingdom royal burial survived so nearly complete. The thousands of objects that were eventually recorded and moved have given people far from Egypt a concrete picture of ancient craft, ritual and daily splendour, and they still prompt fresh study more than a century later.

sources.title: Close Call: How Howard Carter Almost Missed King Tut's Tomb
